title: Life without principle
hookLine: he warns against spending life only to earn a living (Life Without Principle)

lines: A LOAFER, AND AN ENTERPRISING CITIZEN.
cards: Two men in the same woods. One walks there half of every day because he loves them. The other spends his whole day cutting them down for profit.

Which one does the town respect? Thoreau poses almost exactly that question, and answers it: the walker gets called a loafer, and the man clearing the woods, industrious and enterprising. He isn't telling a joke.
He's opening an essay about what a society rewards, and what it quietly calls a waste of time.

teach.b: First, the bustle. The essay is called Life Without Principle, and one of its plainest lines is this: "This world is a place of business. What an infinite bustle!" He says the noise of it wakes him at night.
Trains, trading, hurry; work everywhere, and almost no talk about why.

Second, the loafer and the citizen. His point isn't that work is bad. It's that a life gets measured by what it earns, so the person who loves the woods looks idle and the one who strips them looks useful.

Don't hire someone who does your work only for the money, he says; hire the one who does it for love of it. Pay matters, but a worker's aim should be to do a certain work well, not only to get a living from it.
Fourth, more than a living. The heart of the essay is a worry: that people spend the whole of life getting a living, and never get around to living. Earning money isn't the enemy.

Rent is real, and Thoreau took paid work himself, surveying land among other jobs. But he asks whether anything in your days is something money didn't buy and couldn't: a walk, a friendship, a song you sing to nobody.
It's an uncomfortable essay that doesn't let anyone off easily, its author included. But the question at its center is simple to carry: what in your life is more than a living?

how: Some readers of Life Without Principle take from it a habit of setting aside time for something done for love rather than pay, as a check on letting work fill the whole of life.

games.q: you're hiring someone. one wants the job for the money. one does the work because they love it. who does Thoreau say to choose?

the one who does it for love.
games.why: he says, in effect, hire the one who does it for love of it, not the one who does it only for money.

practice: Let your work, paid or unpaid, settle at the edge of your mind, and ask: what's one thing that earns nothing, done just because it's good?
A walk without a step count, a call to an old friend, ten minutes with a book or a guitar or a garden. Let one thing come, and picture yourself in it.
